Nearly $1 million worth of sports and Pokémon trading cards were stolen from a FedEx truck last week, police in California said Monday. (David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty) Thieves made off with nearly $1 million in sports, Pokémon and other trading cards swiped from a FedEx truck in Southern California last week, police said Monday. Officers responded to a trading card authentication company Tuesday about the theft of an estimated $963,000 worth of cards from a FedEx truck, Santa Ana police spokesperson Natalie Garcia said by email. The theft included two pallets of cards and a third that was “disrupted,” she said. The location of the report was Professional Sports Authenticator in the city of Santa Ana, about 33 miles southeast of Los Angeles. The company bills itself on its website as “the leading third-party authentication and grading service” and says it can sell customers’ cards online for a percentage of the selling price to “turn cards into currency.” Nick Andrews, known on social media as the Boston Card Hunter, said on X that there are multiple victims of the theft, one of whom he said lost $500,000 worth of cards. When all is said and done, he said, the heist could be one of the biggest in trading card history. He has compiled a list of cards claimed to have been taken in the theft that numbered as high as 383 on Monday evening. Among them, as the video game news site IGN noted , were a 1995 Upper Deck 23K Gold Michael Jordan card and a 2024 One Piece Simplified Chinese 1st Anniversary Set Nami. Card trader Sky-B, who said he wants to be referred to only under that moniker, discussed cards he said he lost in the theft in a video on YouTube on Monday. “These were 104 cards that I’ve accumulated over two years,” he said. “There are many irreplaceable cards in here that I will never see again. And, honestly, that’s what hurts the most — outside of obviously being absolutely financially destroyed here.” He said the missing cards were dropped off at Professional Sports Authenticator, where they were certified and started their journey back to him in Michigan before he discovered they had been stolen. Sky-B said he paid $8,000 in grading fees and lamented that he would be out the likely increased value that the grading added to his cards, which he said were insured up to $156,000 — below their likely market value. A company spokesperson said in an email that grading fees would be returned, along with the fair market value of the cards involved. In a statement, the company said it is working with investigators and has deactivated the stolen cards’ certificates. “We have deactivated the certificates for the stolen items and notified marketplace partners so they can be on the lookout for rare and serialized items,” a Professional Sports Authenticator spokesperson said. FedEx said in a statement that getting to the bottom of the theft is paramount. “The security of our customers’ shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation,” it said. Garcia, the police spokesperson, said the value of the stolen goods could rise. “It remains an open case,” she said, “and we have not made any arrests or recovered any stolen goods.” In 2024, a FedEx shipment of 54 vintage baseball cards worth $2.1 million was successfully delivered to a Best Western in Strongsville, Ohio, for a sports card conference, but it was stolen by a hotel employee who was sentenced to four to six years in prison , prosecutors in nearby Cleveland said. item.title: Tensions flare at court hearing on Trump's D.C. golf course renovation
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Golfers play past felled trees at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington D.C., US, on Sunday. - Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg/Getty Images One of the tensest showdowns between the Trump administration and the federal bench in Washington, DC, came to a head on Monday in a marathon court hearing over President Donald Trump’s efforts to overhaul a public golf course that has been the subject of months of litigation. Trump early Monday doubled down on his plan to close and renovate the golf course in Washington, DC, saying construction would begin “IMMEDIATELY” despite a judge’s order to provide three days’ notice ahead of any construction. Trump wrote in a Truth Social post that the government does not “need an approval” to proceed with the construction. “Work is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY! The finished product will be World Class, and bring income and great prestige back to D.C.,” he wrote. By the end of the day, Trump was still fuming about it. Just before midnight, the president posted on Truth Social: “’Trash Island,’ Washington, D.C., the nickname for the broken and dilapidated Golf Course that is the subject of frivolous litigation in the United States Court System, before a judge that seems not to want Greatness for our Capital or our Nation (but who knows?), has been badly managed for so many decades that it is a completely nonviable and unsafe Project.” He said his plan “will turn Trash Island into an Island of Beauty and Success!” But, Trump’s dream of renovating the East Potomac Golf Course is already the subject of a legal fight as preservationists and golfers seek to stop the president from changing the public park. The case may seem relatively minor compared to some of the other sweeping legal battles of Trump’s second term. But the litigation has demanded the attention of several top attorneys from the Justice Department, who have sought to defend the actions government officials who are overseeing the course and have tried distinguish them from the president’s public statements about his intentions for the grounds. US District Judge Ana C. Reyes, who is overseeing the case, issued an order last week that requires the government to give at least three days’ notice before making any “irreparable modification” to the course. Reyes and the third-highest ranking Justice Department official, Associate Attorney General Stan Woodward, sparred repeatedly over the information she was demanding from the administration. The question in the case, since last Monday, had largely been about the administration removing, with less of a day’s notice to the court, of 400-plus trees from the park earlier this month. But the hearing on Monday quickly turned into a clash over what Trump wrote on social media, the Justice Department’s ability to defend separate assertions made by the National Park Service in court, and how far the federal trial-level court can go to demand answers from the executive branch. “I don’t know what to do, when I keep getting different stories,” Reyes told Woodward as the hearing began with a heated moment. “I have, on the one hand the president of the United States saying to the American people … there is a final plan,” Reyes said hours later in the same hearing Monday. “I have you all telling me, witnesses saying what they’re saying, there is no final plan … which is it?” Robert Stander – a DOJ attorney who was handling the bulk of the administration’s legal arguments – struggled to answer the question directly and Reyes rejected his attempts to compare the social media posts to an executive order that was just the start of an agency’s work on a project, rather than a final decision. Woodward returned to the line of questioning at the end of the hearing and told Reyes there was “no plan to close the course, as those words have their literal meaning.” He told the judge that asking Stander, a lower-level attorney that did not go through Senate confirmation, to contradict the president put his colleague in a “difficult” position. Reyes is considering whether to issue a longer-term order limiting what the administration can do to the course, including cutting down more trees. Last week, Reyes presided over a testy hearing in which she said she was “furious” with the administration for removing hundreds of trees without proper notice. The government claimed the removals were routine maintenance unrelated to any plan to renovate the golf course. Reyes ordered that no more trees be cut down before October 26. The Justice Department on Friday filed a motion asking for Reyes’ removal from the case , accusing her of having a “disdain for the Trump Administration.” Reyes over the weekend denied that motion and refuted the government’s claims against her. In his Monday post to Truth Social, Trump disparaged Reyes a “crazed lunatic.” The golf course is one of several renovation projects Trump is working on in Washington. The president’s desire to turn the public course into a professional course – a renovation that could cost between $20 million and $49 million – has angered those who fear it may take away a public and affordable place to play golf in the nation’s capital. Administration officials express ignorance to Trump’s intentions Amid the tense exchanges between DOJ and the judge were hours of testimony from government officials charged with oversight of federal public grounds – testimony that turned the proceedings into a grueling drag through bureaucratic procedures of the National Park Service. Multiple government officials who oversee the golf course expressed ignorance to Trump’s latest assertions about the future of the course. The acting director of the National Park Service, Jessica Bowron – who signed off on this month’s move to cut down the 400-plus trees – said she was not aware of plans to close East Potomac Park next month, nor had she been in any discussions about renovating the course. She and other officials say their work on the removing the trees was carried out under a directive that they implement recommendations from 2019 for making the course look more it did when it was first built, in a proposal known as the Cultural Landscape Report. Reyes has said that she believed that explanation was a pretext for giving the administration cover to start the renovation.
